clinicalPearls: Combined pituitary hormone deficiency denotes impaired secretion of two or more anterior pituitary hormones, most often growth hormone plus one or more of thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotrophic hormone, luteinising/follicle-stimulating hormone and prolactin.

It arises from disordered development of the anterior pituitary, and the pattern and timing of hormone loss depend on which transcription-factor gene is affected (for example PROP1, POU1F1, HESX1, LHX3, LHX4, SOX2, SOX3, OTX2).

Presentation is age-dependent: neonates may show hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, micropenis and undescended testes, whereas older children present with growth failure, delayed or absent puberty and features of hypothyroidism.

The most dangerous deficiency is adrenocorticotrophic hormone deficiency, which can precipitate life-threatening adrenal crisis, especially during intercurrent illness or when thyroxine is started before glucocorticoid cover.
Hormone deficiencies frequently evolve over years, so an initially isolated growth hormone deficiency may progress to involve thyroid, adrenal and gonadal axes, mandating lifelong surveillance.

Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging may reveal a small anterior pituitary, an ectopic or absent posterior pituitary bright spot, an interrupted or thin pituitary stalk, and associated midline or optic-nerve anomalies.

Extra-pituitary features can point to a specific gene, such as a rigid cervical spine and sensorineural deafness in LHX3, or optic-nerve hypoplasia and midline brain defects in HESX1 and septo-optic dysplasia.
Genetic diagnosis guides counselling, informs the expected phenotype and helps anticipate which axes are likely to fail.
reference.pathophysiology: The anterior pituitary develops from Rathke's pouch, an invagination of oral ectoderm, under the control of a tightly ordered cascade of signalling molecules and transcription factors that specify the five hormone-producing cell lineages (somatotrophs, lactotrophs, thyrotrophs, corticotrophs and gonadotrophs). Combined pituitary hormone deficiency results when this programme is disrupted by loss-of-function or dominant-negative mutations in the genes encoding these regulators, so that one or more cell lineages fail to expand, differentiate or survive. Because individual factors act at defined windows and in overlapping domains, the specific gene determines both which lineages are lost and whether the defect is confined to the pituitary or extends to midline forebrain, eye and skeletal structures. Some factors chiefly govern proliferation of pituitary progenitors, so their loss yields a hypoplastic gland, whereas others are needed for terminal differentiation, giving a structurally near-normal gland with selective hormone loss. Progressive apoptosis or failure of stem-cell maintenance explains the characteristic evolution of deficiencies over time. In a large proportion of clinically typical cases no causative mutation is identified, indicating additional undiscovered genes and the contribution of regulatory or oligogenic mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated growth hormone deficiency progressing to further axis involvement
Acquired hypopituitarism from craniopharyngioma or other sellar/suprasellar tumour
Hypopituitarism following cranial irradiation, head injury or infiltrative disease
Septo-optic dysplasia and other midline forebrain malformations
Primary end-organ failure (primary hypothyroidism, primary gonadal failure, primary adrenal insufficiency)
Prader-Willi syndrome and other syndromic causes of growth failure with hypogonadism
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
additionalInvestigations: Baseline anterior pituitary profile with paired target-gland hormones (growth hormone with insulin-like growth factor 1, thyroid-stimulating hormone with free thyroxine, morning cortisol with adrenocorticotrophic hormone, gonadotrophins with sex steroids, prolactin)
Dynamic pituitary testing where indicated (growth hormone stimulation testing, assessment of the adrenal axis)
Dedicated pituitary magnetic resonance imaging with attention to gland size, stalk and posterior pituitary bright spot
Targeted or panel genetic testing of pituitary transcription-factor genes, with array or exome studies in syndromic cases
Formal ophthalmological assessment including optic-disc examination when a midline defect is suspected
Assessment of posterior pituitary function and fluid balance when diabetes insipidus is suspected
Bone age radiograph to quantify skeletal maturation and growth potential
redFlags: Neonatal hypoglycaemia with prolonged jaundice, micropenis or midline facial anomalies suggesting congenital hypopituitarism
Symptoms or signs of adrenal crisis (hypotension, hypoglycaemia, collapse) requiring immediate glucocorticoid
Starting thyroxine replacement before excluding and treating adrenocorticotrophic hormone deficiency, which can precipitate crisis
Rapidly evolving visual failure or headache suggesting an expanding sellar lesion rather than developmental disease
Hyponatraemia or polyuria indicating posterior pituitary or adrenal involvement
reference.prognosis: With timely diagnosis and lifelong, carefully sequenced hormone replacement most individuals achieve near-normal growth, puberty and quality of life. Outcome is compromised mainly by unrecognised or undertreated adrenal insufficiency and by delayed detection of newly evolving deficiencies.
pitfalls: Assuming a single documented deficiency is the whole picture, when further axes commonly fail over subsequent years
Commencing thyroxine before glucocorticoid cover and thereby unmasking or worsening cortisol deficiency
Relying on random hormone levels rather than appropriate dynamic testing and target-gland pairing
Overlooking associated eye, midline brain or skeletal anomalies that indicate a specific genetic cause
Failing to arrange stress dosing and emergency glucocorticoid education for corticotroph deficiency
